title: Research
text: A central through-line of my work explores social epistemology: how cues like language, accent, and race shape children’s inferences about status and competence, and ultimately, determine whose knowledge they trust.

title: Research
text:
Primary Research Themes






The Social Evaluation of Language


How do children evaluate speakers based on the languages they speak or the accents they have? My core programmatic research treats bilingualism as a social category that triggers inferences about competence. While bilingualism is publicly celebrated as an asset, my work investigates the “double standard” where not all bilinguals benefit equally from this prestige.Using forced-choice paradigms and behavioral measures, this work establishes that children generally apply a “more languages = more status” rule, whereas adults hold competing associations of prestige and foreignness. I am currently expanding this line of work in my dissertation to test the mechanisms behind these status attributions—specifically exploring selective trust, cultural learning, and boundary conditions like perceived phenotype. My theoretical work synthesizes how accents function as cues to trust, disentangling theories of social identity from processing fluency.









Trust & Technology: Children’s Perceptions of AI Agents


As artificial intelligence becomes ubiquitous in educational and social contexts, my research asks whether children apply the same human-to-human social reasoning to synthetic voices. Building on findings that accent effects persist with AI-generated audio, this line of work investigates how children evaluate the status of, and selectively learn from, accented AI agents. This research explores critical questions at the intersection of developmental psychology and human-computer interaction, including whether the assumption that AI “knows everything” persists when evaluating accented digital agents.









Racial Socialization


Where do children pick up the social hierarchies that influence their evaluations of others? In collaboration with EmbraceRace, my mixed-methods research analyzes how parents reason about discussing race with their children. By analyzing a nationally representative dataset of U.S. parents, this work challenges prior literature that treats egalitarian beliefs as a universal marker of progressive racial attitudes. Instead, I separate prescriptive egalitarianism (“the world should be equal, so we shouldn’t discuss race”) from descriptive color-consciousness (“the world isn’t equal, so we must discuss it”), revealing how color-evasive ideologies persist even among parents who rate themselves as highly open to discussing race.

title: Alison De Leon Escobar
text: I am a 4th year PhD Candidate in Applied Developmental Psychology at Fordham University researching developmental social cognition. My research utilizes mixed-methods approaches to understand how children and adults reason about groups within social hierarchies.

title: Teaching
text:
NoteTeaching Philosophy



My teaching philosophy centers on making complex psychological and statistical concepts accessible, interactive, and directly applicable to real-world scenarios. I currently serve as the Instructor of Record for Foundations of Psychology, and have extensive experience guiding students through applied data analysis.

title: Teaching
text:
Teaching Assistantships

Introduction to Statistics
Role: Graduate Teaching Assistant
I guided undergraduate students through the practical application of statistical theory, bridging the gap between mathematical formulas and actual data analysis.
Pedagogical Highlights:

Software Proficiency: Instructed students in navigating and running analyses using statistical software, primarily JASP (as well as SPSS).
Applied Analysis: Helped students translate raw data into meaningful psychological insights, focusing on selecting the appropriate statistical tests, interpreting output, and writing up results in APA format.

title: Teaching
text:

Undergraduate Research
Advising undergraduate research assistants Sarah Lorenzo and Debora Cohen, who collaborated on my color-evasiveness project. I am actively supporting them in preparing their findings for presentation at the Fordham Undergraduate Research Symposium.
